newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to spend first full day outside hospital.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to spend first full day outside hospital.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin spends his first full day in his favourite Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow on Saturday, the latest stage in his recovery from a heart operation and on the way back to the Kremlin.

Yeltsin, 65, left the Central Clinical Hospital on Friday and moved to Barvikha, where he is likely to work for up to six hours a day before returning to his Kremlin desk before the end of the year, according to his doctors.
Problems facing Yeltsin, who has been out of the Kremlin since late June, are mounting.
The most urgent is the political crisis in Belarus, which appeared to be all but over on Friday afternoon, when Yeltsin, speaking from Barvikha in a brief television footage, announced:
"The crisis is over. I consider this to be a big victory."

Yeltsin was referring to a deal, mediated by his Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, between hardline Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and leaders of the opposition-dominated parliament over a referendum due on Sunday.
But the Belarussian parliament failed to approve the deal when many deputies blasted it as a sell-out to Lukashenko.
During his television appearence Yeltsin looked much thinner than before his quintuple heart bypass operation but was speaking more clearly, firmly and with strong emotion.

"As a friendly country and as a member of the (Russia-Belarus) community we could not allow Belarus to split. As the president of Russia I could not allow that. That is why we took all the measures we could to find a compromise."
Russia has big political interests in Belarus with which it has formed a loose alliance and Yeltsin may see a continuing crisis there as a personal challenge.
Yeltsin is scheduled to meet the first foreign visitor on Saturday since his operation on November 5 -- Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev.
They are likely to discuss how to strengthen ties inside the Commonwealth of Independent States grouping 12 former Soviet republics and bilateral relations.
Those include the status of the oil-rich Caspian Sea and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, due to pipe Kazakh crude oil to western markets through Russia.
Another tricky issue for Yeltsin is pressure from parliament to remove his powerful chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais.

The State Duma lower house of parliament dealt Yeltsin a blow by urging him to drop Chubais until he has investigated allegations of irregularities in the funding of his re-election campaign this summer.

Chubais, loathed by the opposition communists who dominate the Duma, denied any wrongdoing. He dismissed the allegations as politically motivated by his rivals and said he was ready to answer any questions to help state prosecutors investigate.
On a brighter side, Moscow is close to signing yet another accord with breakaway Chechnya.

Itar-Tass news agency said the agreement was ready for signing by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the head of the Chechen rebel government, Aslan Maskhadov. It is expected to be signed in Moscow soon.
